analysis.one_liner: Sunsets the entire federal income tax code, forcing Congress to write a replacement.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 27 would have ended every federal income tax after 2019, keeping only payroll taxes like Social Security and Medicare contributions. Congress would then have had to pass a brand-new tax system by mid-2019, guided by goals like low rates and no tax on savings. It also required a two-thirds vote in both chambers to push the deadline back. The bill sat in committee and never received a hearing or floor vote before the two-year congressional session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and investors would gain the most, since income taxes on wages, capital gains, and investment income would vanish. Large corporations and tax-advantaged savers would also benefit if the replacement system kept rates low.

how_it_helps.text: Would eliminate all federal income taxes, including taxes on wages, capital gains, and corporate income, after the 2019 tax year.
Sets nonbinding goals for the replacement tax code, favoring low rates and removing taxes on savings and investment income.
Makes it much harder to extend the old tax code by requiring a two-thirds supermajority vote in both chambers to change the termination date.

analysis.who_pays: Whoever ends up paying the replacement taxes. With a single low rate and no tax on investment income, the burden would likely shift from wealthy households toward middle- and lower-income workers through consumption or flat wage taxes, while Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes would continue unchanged.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary wage earners under a new flat tax

drawbacks.text: Repeals the income tax with no guarantee Congress passes a fair replacement in time, risking a chaotic funding gap for federal programs.
The stated goals push toward a flat tax that shields investment and wealth, meaning the tax burden could shift onto working families.
The two-thirds supermajority requirement makes the expiration date nearly impossible to change, forcing the repeal even if no replacement is ready.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promises simplicity and lower rates, but the actual winners would be those with the most income from investments. Ending the income tax without a specific replacement creates serious risk of underfunding the government or shifting taxes onto ordinary workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote, dying when the congressional session ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 6, 2015, the first day of the new Congress, as a statement of principle for tax reform.
Referred jointly to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Rules Committee, where no action was taken.
Gathered 144 cosponsors, almost entirely Republicans, showing strong party support but no path to a floor vote.
Never advanced past committee and expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy households and investors, since the income tax structure they pay most under remained in place and the flat-tax replacement never advanced.

for.name: Bob Goodlatte (R-VA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the Congress and recruited 144 cosponsors.

for.name: House Republicans
for.what_they_did: 144 members cosponsored, showing broad party backing but no committee action followed.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never held a hearing or markup, keeping the bill off the floor.

against.name: Dave Camp (R-CA)
against.what_they_did: As chairman during the first session, chose not to schedule the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 144 cosponsors were Republicans except one Democrat, and the bill never moved past committee.

industries.note: Would eliminate income taxes on wages, capital gains, and investment income; the replacement's stated low-rate goals suggest the burden would fall elsewhere.
Loses its largest revenue source with no guaranteed replacement, risking funding cuts to programs people rely on.
